242: “Beads on a string”: one nucleosome every ≈200 bp, joined by ≈50 bp of linker DNA. In the gene body, nucleosomes (omitted here so the sequence can be read) are taken apart and rebuilt as the polymerase passes, by FACT and SPT6.
244: 147 bp of DNA wrapped 1.65 turns in a left-handed superhelix around a histone octamer: two copies each of H3 (blue), H4 (green), H2A (yellow) and H2B (red). Diameter 11 nm. The N-terminal tails carry the epigenetic marks; here (green beads) H3K4me3 and H3K27ac, signatures of active chromatin.
246: Two antiparallel strands, a right-handed helix 2 nm across, 10.5 bp per turn, 0.34 nm per base pair, major and minor grooves. A (green) pairs with T (red) by 2 hydrogen bonds, G (yellow) with C (blue) by 3.
248: CACCC box (−90, binds the erythroid factor KLF1), CCAAT box (−76, NF-Y) and ATA box (CATAAA, −30, binds TBP). The pre-initiation complex (TFIIA, B, D, E, F, H and Mediator) places RNA polymerase II at the +1 site. Variants here (e.g. c.-78A>G) cause β⁺-thalassaemias.
250: A super-enhancer located ≈50 kb upstream of HBB (hypersensitive sites HS1 to HS5). GATA1, TAL1 and the LDB1 bridge fold it into a loop against the promoter: without it, almost no β-globin.
252: Transcribed but not translated. The +1 site is the A that will receive the cap. The ribosome scans from the cap to the first AUG.
254: Three exons: codons 1–31, 31–105 and 106–147 (HGVS numbering, Met = 1). The pink markers flag classic pathogenic variants: HbS, HbC, HbE and several β-thalassaemias.
257: Contains the polyadenylation signal AATAAA, about twenty nucleotides before the cleavage site. c.*110T>C (AATAAA→AACAAA) causes a β⁺-thalassaemia.
259: After the poly(A) site, the polymerase carries on for a few hundred bp. The exonuclease XRN2 (red) degrades the residual RNA 5′→3′, catches up with the polymerase and dislodges it: the “torpedo” model.
261: 12 subunits, ≈550 kDa. It opens a bubble of ≈12 bp, reads the template strand 3′→5′ and extends the RNA 5′→3′ at ≈30 nt/s (real speed here), after a pause around +40 released by P-TEFb. Its CTD tail (52 YSPTSPS repeats) is phosphorylated on Ser5 (orange: initiation, capping) then Ser2 (cyan: elongation, splicing, cleavage).
262: U1 recognises the GU donor site (light blue), U2 the branch A (green), U2AF the AG acceptor site. The U4/U6·U5 tri-snRNP completes the spliceosome (mauve): two transesterifications release the intron as a lariat and join the exons. An EJC complex (pink) is deposited 20–24 nt upstream of each junction.
264: 7-methylguanosine cap + CBC complex (white) from 25 nt. Gold exons, blue introns, green poly(A) tail (≈200 A added by poly(A) polymerase after cleavage by CPSF). Splicing is co-transcriptional.
265: Mature mRNA: 626 nt + poly(A), compacted with CBC, EJC and PABPN1. The TREX complex recruits the export receptor NXF1–NXT1; through the pore, cap first, along an interchromatin channel. Follow it!
267: Five ribosomes translate the mRNA at ≈5 codons/s: 147 codons, a β chain of 146 amino acids once the initial Met is removed (red dot = nascent chain). 2 α + 2 β + 4 haems = haemoglobin A.
275: c.20A>T p.(Glu7Val): HbS, sickle cell disease

304: A biconcave disc of ≈ 7.8 µm, with no nucleus or organelles, ≈ 2.5 µm thick at the rim and ≈ 1 µm at the centre: a large exchange surface and high deformability, letting it through capillaries narrower than itself. It holds ≈ 270 million haemoglobin molecules (≈ 30 pg) and lives ≈ 120 days. Under its membrane, a spectrin network tethered by ankyrin and protein 4.1 gives it shape and elasticity; band 3 exchanges Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻.
305: An anucleate megakaryocyte fragment, discoid, 2 to 3 µm. α granules (von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, PDGF) and dense granules (ADP, serotonin, Ca²⁺). Activated by collagen or thrombin, it changes shape, aggregates through integrin αIIbβ3 and fibrinogen, and starts haemostasis. Lifespan: 7 to 10 days.
308: You are in the red marrow, between bone trabeculae: every day it produces ≈ 200 billion red cells, more than 100 billion platelets and about 100 billion neutrophils. In front of you, an erythroblastic island — a macrophage surrounded by erythroblasts at every stage — next to a sinusoid. The small bilobed proteins near the target cell are holo-transferrins (80 kDa, 2 Fe³⁺). Licence: real marrow is very dense; cells are spread apart here so that you can move around.
310: A wide capillary (≈ 20 µm) with a very thin wall: a single layer of endothelial cells, a discontinuous basal lamina and adventitial reticular cells. It is the exit door of the marrow: mature blood cells cross it through the very body of endothelial cells, via transient pores. Plasma proteins, including transferrin, cross it freely: the ship gets through when it is small.
312: Plasma (≈ 55 % of blood volume): water, albumin (≈ 40 g/L), immunoglobulins, fibrinogen, lipoproteins, transferrin (2 to 3 g/L, about one third saturated with iron). Cells: ≈ 5 million red cells, 150,000 to 400,000 platelets and 4,000 to 10,000 leukocytes per microlitre. The “Travel by blood” button takes you to another organ.
314: A red cell that has just lost its nucleus. It still has ribosomes, globin mRNAs, a few mitochondria and transferrin receptors, which it eliminates in 2 to 3 days (autophagy, exosomes) while remodelling its membrane; it spends the last day in the blood, after crossing the sinusoid endothelium. 0.5 to 2 % of circulating red cells are reticulocytes: their count reflects erythropoietic activity.
315: Central macrophage of the erythroblastic island
316: At the heart of the island, it holds a ring of erythroblasts against itself with adhesion molecules (VCAM-1 on the macrophage, integrin α4β1 on the erythroblast; EMP protein). It engulfs the expelled nuclei, which expose phosphatidylserine, and digests them with the DNase II of its lysosomes. Macrophages also recycle iron from old red cells: exported by ferroportin, it is picked up again by transferrin. The island was described by Marcel Bessis in 1958.
